source: OMB, Analytical Perspectives FY2027, Table 10-1 (tax expenditures)

breaks.name: Exclusion for employer-provided health insurance
breaks.desc: Health insurance premiums paid by employers aren't counted as taxable income for workers. It's the largest tax break, and it encourages more generous job-based coverage. Repealing it would also raise payroll taxes, which this estimate doesn't include. CBO's option to cap it instead (at the 50th percentile of premiums) raises about $1.2 trillion over 10 years.
omb: 130: Exclusion of employer contributions for medical insurance premiums and medical care

breaks.name: Employer retirement plans (401(k)s and pensions)
breaks.desc: Contributions to 401(k)s and pensions, and their investment earnings, aren't taxed until withdrawal. OMB's estimate counts this year's deferral, but much of it is repaid later when retirees pay tax on withdrawals, so the true long-run gain from repeal is smaller.
omb: 149: Defined contribution employer plans
148: Defined benefit employer plans

breaks.name: IRAs and self-employed retirement plans
breaks.desc: Tax deferral on Individual Retirement Accounts and plans for the self-employed. As with employer plans, part of this revenue would be collected later anyway when money is withdrawn.
omb: 150: Individual Retirement Accounts
153: Self-Employed plans

breaks.name: Capital gains exclusion on home sales
breaks.desc: Homeowners can exclude up to $250,000 ($500,000 for couples) of profit when they sell their main home.
omb: 64: Capital gains exclusion on home sales

breaks.name: 20% deduction for pass-through business income
breaks.desc: Owners of partnerships, S corporations, and sole proprietorships can deduct up to 20% of their business income (Section 199A). The 2025 law made it permanent. Most of the benefit goes to high-income owners.
omb: 83: Allow 20-percent deduction to certain pass-through income

breaks.name: Accelerated depreciation (immediate expensing of equipment)
breaks.desc: Businesses can deduct the cost of equipment immediately instead of over its useful life. The 2025 law made 100% 'bonus depreciation' permanent. Because it shifts deductions earlier rather than eliminating them, repeal raises most in the first years.
omb: 80: Accelerated depreciation of machinery and equipment (normal tax method)

breaks.name: Charitable contribution deductions
breaks.desc: Itemizers can deduct donations to charities, schools, and hospitals. The 2025 law adds a small deduction for non-itemizers and a 0.5%-of-income floor starting in 2026.
omb: 123: Deductibility of charitable contributions, other than education and health
109: Deductibility of charitable contributions to educational institutions
137: Deductibility of charitable contributions to health institutions

breaks.name: State and local tax (SALT) deduction
breaks.desc: Itemizers can deduct state and local income (or sales) and property taxes. The 2025 law raised the cap from $10,000 to $40,000 through 2029 for most taxpayers.
omb: 62: Deductibility of State and local property tax on owner-occupied homes
174: Deductibility of nonbusiness State and local taxes other than on owner-occupied homes

breaks.name: Mortgage interest deduction
breaks.desc: Itemizers can deduct interest on up to $750,000 of mortgage debt on a first or second home.
omb: 61: Deductibility of mortgage interest on owner-occupied homes

breaks.name: Tax-free interest on state and local bonds
breaks.desc: Interest on most bonds issued by states and cities isn't federally taxed, which lowers their borrowing costs. Repeal would raise costs for state and local governments.
omb: 172: Exclusion of interest on public purpose State and local bonds

breaks.name: Partial exclusion of Social Security benefits
breaks.desc: Up to 85% of Social Security benefits are taxable, and only for people with income above fixed thresholds that have never been indexed to inflation. Taxing benefits like pensions would raise revenue, much of it credited to the Social Security and Medicare trust funds.
omb: 166: Social Security benefits for retired and disabled workers and spouses, dependents and survivors

breaks.name: Child tax credit (the part that reduces income tax)
breaks.desc: The $2,200-per-child credit, to the extent it reduces income tax owed. The refundable part paid to families who owe little tax is spending, under Income Security on the Spending tab.
omb: 141: Child credit

breaks.name: Research and development tax breaks
breaks.desc: The research credit plus immediate deduction of research costs, which the 2025 law restored for domestic research.
omb: 8: Credit for increasing research activities
7: Expensing of research and experimentation expenditures (normal tax method)

breaks.name: Deduction for export-related income (FDII/FDDEI)
breaks.desc: A lower tax rate on U.S. companies' income from serving foreign markets, meant to keep intellectual property in the U.S.
omb: 5: Deduction for foreign-derived intangible income derived from trade or business within the United States

breaks.name: Exclusion of life insurance death benefits
breaks.desc: Life insurance payouts to beneficiaries aren't taxed.
omb: 55: Exclusion of life insurance death benefits

breaks.name: Low-Income Housing Tax Credit
breaks.desc: Credits for investors who build or renovate affordable rental housing. The 2025 law expanded it. Repeal would reduce affordable housing construction.
omb: 67: Credit for low-income housing investments

breaks.name: Health savings accounts
breaks.desc: Contributions to HSAs paired with high-deductible health plans are tax-free, as are withdrawals for medical expenses.
omb: 132: Medical Savings Accounts / Health Savings Accounts

breaks.name: Clean energy tax credits (what remains after 2025)
breaks.desc: Credits for wind, solar, nuclear, clean fuels, hydrogen, advanced manufacturing, and home energy efficiency. The 2025 law phased many of them out early; this is what remains.

breaks.name: 2025 law's temporary deductions (tips, overtime, car loans, seniors)
breaks.desc: Deductions for tip income, overtime pay, interest on loans for new U.S.-assembled cars, and an extra $6,000 deduction for people 65 and older. All expire after 2028 under current law, so ending them early raises money only through 2028.
